Practice Quizzes and Retention of Science Vocabulary in Seventh Graders

Introduction
Teachers often ask students to reread a text to prepare for a test. Research on memory suggests that practicing retrieval may help more than rereading. In this study, researchers tested the hypothesis that taking a practice quiz leads to better retention of science vocabulary than rereading the same material.

Participants
The 120 participants were seventh graders from two public middle schools in one mid-sized city. All students whose parents returned a permission form and who agreed to take part were included. A computer randomly assigned the students to the Quiz group (60 students) or the Reread group (60 students).

All students studied a 20-term science vocabulary text for 15 minutes. The Quiz group then spent 10 minutes taking a practice quiz on the terms, and the Reread group spent 10 minutes rereading the text. One week later, all students took a 20-item test in which they wrote the definition of each term. Retention was defined as the number of the 20 terms that a student defined correctly on the one-week test.

The study was approved by the school district's institutional review board. Parents gave written permission, and each student gave verbal agreement and was told that he or she could stop at any time without penalty. Students' tests were labeled with code numbers rather than names.

The table shows the results. The researchers reported that the difference between the groups was statistically significant.

Sleep Duration and Daily Mood in Ninth Graders

Introduction
Many teenagers sleep less than experts recommend. This study examined the hypothesis that ninth graders who sleep longer on school nights report better mood the next day than ninth graders who sleep less.

Each student wore a wrist sleep monitor for 14 school nights. The monitor recorded the minutes between falling asleep and waking up. A Large Request First: Compliance With a Small Request Among Shoppers

Introduction
Compliance techniques can change how likely a person is to agree to a request. This study tested the hypothesis that people who first refuse a very large request will be more likely to agree to a smaller request than people who are asked only the smaller request.

Participants
The 160 participants were adult shoppers approached in the entrance of a large shopping center in one city on weekday afternoons. A researcher approached every shopper who walked alone toward the entrance. Shoppers were randomly assigned by a coin flip to the Large-then-small group (80 shoppers) or the Small-only group (80 shoppers).

Procedure
A trained researcher asked shoppers in the Large-then-small group to volunteer 10 hours a month for a local food bank. When the shopper refused, the researcher asked the shopper to donate five minutes to help sort donated cans at a table that day. Shoppers in the Small-only group were asked only to donate five minutes. Compliance was defined as the shopper agreeing and walking to the table within one minute.

Ethical procedures
The shopping center and a university institutional review board approved the study. Because no personal information was recorded, shoppers were not asked for their names. After the five-minute activity, or after a shopper declined, the researcher explained the true purpose of the study, said that no one was required to continue, and offered a card with the research team's contact information.

The table shows the number of shoppers in each group who complied.

ALTON original source — a summary of a (fictional) peer-reviewed study.

A Mindfulness Course and Test Anxiety in Community College Students

Introduction
Test anxiety can interfere with performance. This study tested the hypothesis that a short mindfulness course reduces test anxiety.

Participants
The 80 participants were students at one community college who responded to a campus announcement asking for students who felt anxious before tests. A computer randomly assigned 40 students to a four-week mindfulness course and 40 students to a waiting-list group that took the course after the study.

Procedure
Before and after the four weeks, all students completed a 20-item questionnaire about their anxiety before tests. Each item was rated from 1 (never) to 5 (always), so scores could range from 20 to 100, with higher scores meaning more anxiety. Test anxiety was defined as a student's total score on the 20-item questionnaire.

Ethical procedures
A college institutional review board approved the study. Students signed informed consent forms that described the course and the waiting list, and they were told they could stop at any time. Questionnaires were identified by code numbers, and counseling center information was given to every student.

Results
The table shows the mean questionnaire score for each group before and after the four weeks.

payload.title: Phones in class
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A laboratory experiment on notifications
Researchers randomly assigned 90 high school students to listen to a 20-minute recorded lecture in one of two conditions. In the Silent condition (45 students), phones were turned off and kept in a bag. In the Notification condition (45 students), students' own phones were on the desk and sent six standard notification sounds during the lecture. All students then took a 20-question quiz on the lecture. The mean quiz score was 78 percent in the Silent condition and 66 percent in the Notification condition. The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A survey of students and teachers
Researchers surveyed 600 students and 120 teachers in six schools. Of the students, 58 percent said that they check their phones at least five times during a typical class, and 44 percent said that having their phone during class helps them feel less anxious. Of the teachers, 71 percent said that phones distract students during lessons. The researchers noted that participants who volunteered to answer the survey may feel more strongly about phones than others.

Source 3: A comparison of schools with and without phone bans
Researchers compared the mean end-of-year math scores in 20 schools that banned phones during class and 20 similar schools that did not. Schools were not assigned to the bans. The mean score was 2 points higher (out of 100) in the schools with bans, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = .21). The researchers reported that the effect size was small.

ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A survey of alumni
Researchers surveyed 800 adults who graduated from high school five years earlier. Of the 400 who had completed required service hours in high school, 46 percent reported volunteering in the past year. Researchers randomly assigned 120 students at one school to a Required group (60 students), who had to complete 20 service hours, or an Optional group (60 students), who were invited to complete service hours if they wished. Researchers interviewed 40 students about their service experiences. Of the 40, 28 said that after helping at a local shelter they felt more confident that they could make a difference in their community. Fifteen of those who completed required hours described the hours as 'something I had to get done.' The researchers noted that students who agreed to be interviewed may have had stronger opinions than others.

ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A laboratory experiment
Researchers randomly assigned 100 adults to learn 60 unfamiliar foreign words in one of two ways. The Massed group (50 adults) studied the words in one 60-minute session. The Spaced group (50 adults) studied for 20 minutes on each of three days. All participants were tested on the words one week later. The mean number of words recalled was 21 in the Massed group and 33 in the Spaced group. The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A classroom study of weekly quizzes
In one school district, 12 history classes were randomly selected to give a short cumulative quiz each week (Quiz classes), and 12 classes used no weekly quizzes (No-quiz classes). The same teacher taught one Quiz class and one No-quiz class, and all classes took the same final exam. The mean final exam score was 84 percent in the Quiz classes and 78 percent in the No-quiz classes. The researchers reported that the difference was statistically significant.

Source 3: A survey of study habits
Researchers surveyed 500 high school students. Of the students, 70 percent said that studying a lot the night before a test works better than studying a little each day. When the researchers compared the students' reported study methods with their exam grades, they found that students who reported studying a little each day earned higher grades on average than students who reported cramming. Students who volunteered for the survey were more likely to be in advanced classes.

payload.title: Team bonuses
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A laboratory experiment on effort
Researchers asked 80 students to pull on a rope-pulling machine that measured force. In the Alone condition (40 students), each student believed that his or her own force was measured. In the Team condition (40 students), each student believed that only the total force of a four-person team was measured. Students in the Alone condition produced a mean force of 100 units, and students in the Team condition produced a mean force of 78 units. The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A survey of employee burnout
Researchers surveyed 500 employees at a large company about their workload and their sense of burnout. Employees who said that the amount of work in their team was shared unfairly reported more burnout, and the correlation between perceived unfairness of workload and burnout was r = +0.44. Employees who volunteered to answer the survey were more likely to work in teams that rewarded group results.

Source 3: A field study of two sales offices
Researchers compared two sales offices of the same company for one year. Office A paid a bonus based on each salesperson's own sales (individual bonus), and Office B paid a bonus based on the sales of the entire office (team bonus). Office A's mean monthly sales per person were $52,000 and Office B's were $47,000. Employees were not randomly assigned to the offices, and Office B was in a region with lower average incomes.
